title: Your home's customs
hookLine: every home develops its own customs
tomorrow: a man sleeps for years and wakes up knowing no one. then what?

lines: PANCAKES ON THE FIRST SNOW DAY.
cards: Plenty of families have one: pancakes on the first snow day, a song in the car on the way to Grandma's, a chair nobody but Dad sits in. Nobody remembers who started it, and nobody would dare stop.
Jewish life has a word for those: minhag, custom. And the tradition takes them more seriously than you might expect.

teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Beitzah, tells of a message the sages in the land of Israel sent to Jews living far away, about a custom they kept.
The message: be careful with the custom of your ancestors, which is in your hands. Not a commandment, a custom, and still held in both hands. Customs come in every size.
Some are shared by whole communities.
Some live in one kitchen: the melody a grandmother used for Kiddush, the order in which people light the candles, the blessing whispered after the hands come off a child's head.
A home grows its own over the years, often by accident. The tradition holds them dearly and lightly at once. A custom isn't a commandment, so it can bend.
But it's yours to carry, and a new one can begin any week.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's advice about a family custom is to keep it in your hands.

how: Jewish communities keep their own minhagim, such as different melodies, holiday foods and prayer orders among Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, and families keep their own, passed down at the Shabbat and holiday table.

o: a family's tradition of moving every few years
the laws a rabbi sets for each household
the customs a home grows and hands down

games.q: custom and commandment — tap the pairs.
p: your ancestors' custom, in your hands

s: a custom carries exactly the same weight as a commandment
a minhag isn't a mitzvah, so it can bend; it's still held dearly.
the Talmud tells communities to keep their ancestors' customs in their hands
Beitzah: be careful with the custom of your ancestors.
only old customs count; a family can't start a new one
a home grows its own, and a new one can begin any week.

games.q: you and your partner grew up lighting Hanukkah candles in different ways. your new home has to pick. what fits today's lesson?
o: choose together, or keep both; a home grows its own customs.
use whichever family's way is older, no matter what.
drop both; customs aren't really part of the tradition.
games.why: customs are held dearly and lightly at once: yours to carry, and yours to grow.

practice: Write down by hand one custom your home already has, or one you'd like to begin: small is fine, a song, a dish, a word at the door. Underneath it, write one name: the person you'd hand it to someday.

wordCard.voice: Your home's customs: minhag, the habits a home grows on its own, held in your hands like your ancestors' customs.

orig.note: Hebrew: custom; the plural is minhagim.

carryVoice: For the road: your own customs, small enough to keep and big enough to hand on. Fifteen of fifteen; home and family, complete.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Beitzah 4b (be careful with the custom of your ancestors, which is in your hands)
